candidates.label: Babylon (Mesopotamia, near Hillah)
candidates.support: The ruins of the Mesopotamian capital, on the Euphrates near modern Hillah, Iraq, are the undisputed site of the ancient city Matthew and Acts recall as the place of Judah's exile; some scholars also read this as the literal place meant by "Babylon" in 1 Peter 5:13, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes there is no tradition connecting the apostle Peter with this city, and that Josephus records most of its Jewish population had already been driven out to neighboring towns by this period. Wikidata and Pleiades's coordinates for the site agree closely.

candidates.label: Babylon Fortress, Old Cairo
candidates.support: A Roman fortress in what is now Old Cairo, Egypt, which the first-century geographer Strabo says was founded by refugees from the Mesopotamian Babylon; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records this as one of three historic proposals for the "Babylon" of 1 Peter 5:13, but judges it improbable, since in the first century the fortress was little more than a military post, and no tradition connects the apostle Peter with Egypt.

unmappedCandidates.label: Rome (figurative name, in 1 Peter and Revelation)
unmappedCandidates.support: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reports that most scholars, from at least the time of the early Christian writer Tertullian onward, have read "Babylon" in Revelation as a figurative name for Rome, citing features of the "Babylon" Revelation describes, such as ruling over "the kings of the earth" and sitting on "seven mountains," that fit Rome rather than any other city of that age; the same encyclopedia reports that most interpreters before the Reformation likewise read 1 Peter 5:13's "Babylon" as Rome, partly because Peter's letter also sends greetings from Mark, who other New Testament letters place with Paul in Rome.
unmappedCandidates.reason: A figurative reading of Rome, a place that has its own record in this project; no separate coordinate is needed here.

unmappedCandidates.label: Jerusalem (minor figurative reading)
unmappedCandidates.support: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a few interpreters have read Revelation's "Babylon" as a figurative name for Jerusalem rather than Rome, though it records that most scholars reject this reading.
unmappedCandidates.reason: A minor figurative reading of Jerusalem, a place that has its own record in this project; no separate coordinate is needed here.

summary.text: Babylon was the capital of ancient Mesopotamia, on the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad, and the city to which the kingdom of Judah was exiled in the sixth century BC; Matthew's genealogy and Stephen's speech in Acts both recall this exile by name. Revelation names "Babylon" repeatedly as a doomed city, in terms most scholars read as a figurative name for Rome rather than a reference to the Mesopotamian city itself. Where Peter wrote that "she who is in Babylon" sends greetings, in 1 Peter 5:13, is disputed: proposals include Rome (read figuratively, the traditional and most widely held view), the Mesopotamian city itself, and a Roman fortress in Egypt called Babylon, near modern Cairo.

history.text: Matthew's genealogy of Jesus marks "the exile to Babylon" as a hinge point, counting fourteen generations from Abraham to the exile and fourteen more from the exile to Jesus; in Stephen's speech in Acts, he tells the Jewish council that because Israel worshiped false gods, God said he would "carry you away beyond Babylon."

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia sets out three historic proposals for the "Babylon" from which 1 Peter was written: the Mesopotamian city, the Egyptian fortress near Old Cairo, and Rome read figuratively. It judges the Egyptian option improbable, since Babylon in Egypt was by then little more than a military station with no tradition of a visit by Peter; it notes that some reputable scholars have held the Mesopotamian reading, but that Josephus records most of that city's Jewish community had already been driven out to neighboring towns by this period, with no evidence of a church there or of any visit by Peter. The encyclopedia concludes that internal evidence, including the letter's greeting from Mark, favors Rome, and that this figurative reading was the common view of the church before the Reformation.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes every reference to "Babylon" in Revelation as figurative, noting that the name is explicitly called a "mystery" at Revelation 17:5; it reports that this figurative Babylon has, since at least the time of the early Christian writer Tertullian, most often been read as Rome, an identification adopted by the early Christian writers Jerome and Augustine and commonly accepted by the church since.

scripture.textWEB: Josiah became the father of Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the exile to Babylon. After the exile to Babylon, Jechoniah became the father of Shealtiel. Shealtiel became the father of Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel became the father of Abiud. Abiud became the father of Eliakim. Eliakim became the father of Azor. Azor became the father of Zadok. Zadok became the father of Achim. Achim became the father of Eliud. Eliud became the father of Eleazar. Eleazar became the father of Matthan. Matthan became the father of Jacob. Jacob became the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ. So all the generations from Abraham to David are fourteen generations; from David to the exile to Babylon fourteen generations; and from the carrying away to Babylon to the Christ, fourteen generations.
You took up the tabernacle of Moloch, the star of your god Rephan, the figures which you made to worship, so I will carry you away beyond Babylon.’
She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you. So does Mark, my son.

otConnections.note: 2 Kings records King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon's siege and eventual destruction of Jerusalem, the exile Matthew's genealogy and Stephen's speech both recall.

Daniel records King Nebuchadnezzar surveying his capital and asking, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built?"; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia cites this verse as a fitting summary of Nebuchadnezzar's own building work at the city.
